name: Self-propaganda
statement: Self-propaganda is the name given to talking oneself into a belief and then refusing the evidence against it, and no effect is measured under that name.
meaning: The label describes an outcome and names other people's mechanisms to explain it. Its Wikipedia article attributes the process to confirmation bias, cognitive dissonance and communal reinforcement, and offers filter bubbles and echo chambers as examples. Each of those has a research literature, and three of them have entries here. What the label adds is a heading. It states no prediction that distinguishes it from selective exposure, from dissonance reduction, or from self-persuasion, which is the studied case of a person moving their own attitude by producing the argument for it. A term that can only be tested by testing something else is a summary rather than a claim, and the measurements below belong to the things it summarises.

origin.who: an anonymous Wikipedia editor writing as Slokunshialgo
origin.note: No coining publication was located. The first revision of the Wikipedia article, timestamped 7 March 2006, carried no citations and was tagged as a psychology stub. It defined the term as ordinary propaganda "done to oneself" and said the person "will go over every aspect of their side of the 'argument'" and "refuse to look at any alternatives". The article has carried a "more citations needed" banner dated May 2010 since then. It sits in Wikipedia's Category:Cognitive biases, and the word does not appear in Wikipedia's own List of cognitive biases.

evidence: The article's own references are a cognitive therapy volume, a book on propaganda in the helping professions, a graduate thesis, a newspaper opinion column and two magazine pieces. None reports a study of self-propaganda, and none was obtained for this entry. What has been measured is selective exposure, the preference for information that agrees with one's existing position. Hart, Albarracin, Eagly, Brechan, Lindberg and Merrill collected 67 eligible reports containing 91 studies, which supplied 300 statistically independent groups and just under 8,000 participants. The average effect was d = 0.36, 95% CI [0.34, 0.39] by fixed-effects analysis and d = 0.38, 95% CI [0.32, 0.44] by random effects, with an unweighted mean of 0.38. Effect sizes were heterogeneous. The preference weakened where participants' views had been supported before they chose, where those views were not tied to their values or held with conviction, where the available information was of low quality, and where their confidence was high. It reversed into a preference for disagreeable information when that information helped accomplish a current goal. The authors close the abstract by noting that diverse information in an environment does not guarantee diverse views.

replication.headline: No study of self-propaganda was found, because nothing is operationalised under the name. Its components are measured, and two of those measurements cut against the popular account.
replication.detail: Crossref returns no work on the term, whether searched bibliographically or by title. Semantic Scholar returns no result set for it. Europe PMC and PubMed return papers on propaganda and on self-persuasion, and none on self-propaganda. Two adjacent results contradict the label as written. Wikipedia calls self-propaganda a form of self-deception; Zhang and Rand ran two preregistered experiments, at 1,609 and 2,399 participants, comparing an incentivised persuasion task with an incentivised summary task, found the same amount of belief shift in both, and report that completing the summary task first cut the later shift roughly fivefold. Their conclusion is that the shift comes from exposure to goal-aligned arguments rather than from a motive to deceive oneself. Wikipedia also offers the Facebook filter bubble as a case. Nyhan and 29 colleagues measured that the median US Facebook user in 2020 saw 50.4% of their content from like-minded sources against 14.7% from cross-cutting ones, then ran a field experiment on 23,377 consenting users. Between 24 September and 23 December 2020 the intervention pushed like-minded exposure down to 36.2% in the treatment group while the control group held at 53.7%. Eight preregistered attitudinal measures, among them affective polarisation, ideological extremity and belief in false claims, did not move.

limits: The search covered Crossref by bibliographic and title query, Semantic Scholar, PubMed, Europe PMC and general web search. OpenAlex was not searched, because its API refused the request for want of quota, and no psychology-specific database such as PsycINFO was searched. Absence of a study is a statement about those places. Nothing here settles whether the term has a longer history outside indexed journals, and the six references on the Wikipedia article were not obtained: three sit behind Google Books previews or an institutional proxy, one is a university thesis and one link is dead. Zhang and Rand were read in abstract at Europe PMC and not in full, so the fivefold figure is their own summary of Study 2. DiFonzo and colleagues' 2013 paper is closed, Unpaywall lists no open copy, and it is named on this page without being read. Hart and colleagues were read in full from the author manuscript at PMC, and Nyhan and colleagues in full at Nature. Neither study was designed to test self-propaganda, and both are cited here for the components the label borrows rather than as verdicts on it.
misreadings: The first misreading is that the term marks a distinct finding. It marks a folder. Its own page explains it by confirmation bias, cognitive dissonance and communal reinforcement, which is a list of other topics rather than a mechanism. The second is that it is self-deception under another name. Zhang and Rand's preregistered studies locate the effect in what arguments a person is exposed to, and an incentive to persuade was not needed to produce it. The third is that echo chambers demonstrate it. Cutting like-minded content by about a third for three months changed what 23,377 Facebook users saw and left all eight preregistered attitude measures where they were. The fourth concerns the one named psychologist on the page. Wikipedia's claim that Nicholas DiFonzo found partisans polarising when segregated and less so when mixed is sourced to a 2011 New York Times opinion column. A peer-reviewed paper by DiFonzo and seven colleagues on rumour clustering and polarisation exists in the Journal of Experimental Social Psychology, and it is not the citation the page gives. The fifth is that selective exposure is unconditional. Hart and colleagues found the preference reversing where uncongenial information served a goal the person had.

sources.text: Wikipedia, Self-propaganda. The article that carries the term as a cognitive bias. Used to find the claims examined above and quoted as their carrier, not relied on for any finding.
